Chamonix mayor plans tourist limits for Alpine beauty spot

Rising numbers around Lac Blanc are having big impact on environment and on visitors’ enjoyment, mayor says

In the Alpine town of Chamonix, most tourist paths lead to the national park with spectacular views across Mont Blanc and the shrinking blue glaciers. In the summer, up to 4,000 tourists a day hike or take the cable car to the lakes high in the Aiguilles Rouges nature reserve.

Many of them descend disappointed. Once a place of nature and tranquility, the beauty spot’s visitor numbers have more than doubled since 2020, spoiling the experience and leaving trails of litter, threatening the environment and wildlife.

Now Chamonix plans to become the first town in the Alps to introduce visitor quotas, to limit the number of hikers around Lac Blanc and the Lacs des Chéserys.

The town’s mayor, Francois-Xavier Laffin, announced last week that from next June tourists would be required to book in advance to visit the area. After booking, they will receive a QR code granting them access.

People visit the ice cave of the Mer de Glace glacier in Chamonix. Photograph: Delpixart/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Laffin championed the quotas after visiting Marseille, where a similar scheme was introduced limiting access to the Calanques national park in 2022. He said the aim was “reserve to preserve”, adding that visiting the mountains would still be free but subject to conditions.

Laffin said mass tourism was having a major impact on the environment, wildlife and on visitors’ enjoyment of the reserve. “Lac Blanc is one place we cannot let continue to deteriorate” he said, adding that the council was looking at additional regulations in other areas.

The plan, which needs the final approval of the local prefect, would restrict the number of visitors to the Lac Blanc area to between 600 and 1,000 a day for four months from June to September.

Christian Schwoehrer, the director of the Haute-Savoie Nature Conservation Agency, which manages the reserve, said: “We will see how it works for the next three years and if it does then it will be extended and maybe applied to other areas. This is a nature reserve but when there are thousands of visitors a day there’s no peace for the protected species or local people and we need stronger measures to control this.

“At points of entry [to the reserve] there will be ‘eco guards’ to verify that people have reserved. If they haven’t, they could be fined, though our intention is to avoid fining people by making sure they know in advance and cannot say they weren’t warned.”

Visitors near Lac Blanc in the Aiguilles Rouge nature reserve above Chamonix. Photograph: Simon Turner/Alamy

The quota plan has met some local opposition from the land’s legal owners. Lac Blanc sits in just under 3 square miles of private estate held by 35 families under a historic entity that has existed for centuries and is now managed by the Montagne de Chéserys company.

One of the landowners, Guillaume Ravanel, a mountain guide, agreed tourist numbers need controlling but suggested visitors should be asked to pay a small entry fee to access the reserve.

Frédéric Charlet-Berguerand, a co-manager of Montagne de Chéserys, told Le Monde: “This quota system is innovative and virtuous.” Contacted by the Guardian, he added: “That said, there will be no quotas on our private property until they are approved by a meeting of the owners,” due to be held in December. “Let’s not put the cart before the horse.”

The mayor is also looking at tighter controls on the Ultra-Trail du Mont Blanc. Photograph: AscentXmedia/Getty Images

Laffin said the quota plan would cost about €590,000 for the three-year “experimental” period. Financing has yet to be arranged but he said part would be raised by Chamonix and other local authorities and the town would be applying for a grant from the government’s “green fund” to help protect the environment. Private sponsors are also being sought.

The mayor, elected in March, has made managing tourist numbers a priority. He is also looking at tighter controls on the three-week Ultra-Trail du Mont Blanc, an ultramarathon circling the Mont-Blanc massif through France, Italy and Switzerland that begins in Chamonix. The event, started in 2003, now attracts 10,000 runners and up to 50,000 visitors each August.

Schwoehrer said summer crowds meant local people were avoiding the reserve. A recent survey found that 55% of visitors who ascended to Lac Blanc said they were disappointed by the experience, he said.

“We don’t want to stop people going there, just have a few stronger rules. It’s a compromise to ensure that visitors have a good experience and at the same time the natural environment is protected.”

We have to show Putin that his attempts to weaken our support will fail.” “Our citizens need to know that the lights will stay on, that their homes will stay warm, that hospitals, transport and communications will keep working.” “One day it can be in the form of an arson attack against a factory or drones disrupt disrupting an airport. The next, it is sabotaged railways or cargo vessels targeted at sea and cyber-attacks.” “It’s all happening now, and it won’t go away anytime soon. … The conclusion of all of this is that we are all targeted, that we are all affected – when it comes to our pipelines, our cables, our energy grids and our economies – and they are all interconnected. … That means that we are all in this for the long term, and therefore we must step up to the plate, to ensure that, we stay ahead of danger.” “But if we are serious about keeping our alliance strong and secure, then all allies must pull their weight not only in 2035, but starting now. At least, everybody needs to have the credible path to get there.” “These investments are also a boon to prosperity. There are dividends to be gained from investing more in defence. Compass may move its primary listing to the US as soon as Tuesday. Photograph: Dado Ruvić/Reuters

NHS caterer Compass ‘plans stock market switch’ in blow to London

Surrey-based firm’s decision to move primary listing to New York would mark latest loss for FTSE 100

• Business live – latest updates

Compass, one of the biggest companies in the FTSE 100, is reportedly planning to switch its primary listing from London to the US in the latest hit to the struggling UK stock market.

The £43.6bn ($57bn) catering giant, which has been listed in London since 1988, could announce its intention to move its listing to New York as soon as Tuesday when it reports its annual results, according to the Financial Times.

The caterer is a major government contractor, providing meals in more than 2,000 schools, academies, colleges and universities across the UK and in some NHS hospitals, as well as offices in the private sector.

It also provides grab-and-go foods for fast food chains and cafes such as Starbucks, Costa and Taco Bell. Last year, the company made about three-quarters of its $3bn profit in North America.

Compass, which switched its reporting currency from British sterling to US dollars in October 2023, also changed the trading currency of its London-listed shares to US dollars in April this year.

The company, which is headquartered in Surrey and has more than 600,000 staff around the world, plans to retain a secondary listing in London and will say that there is no threat to its staff in the UK, according to the Telegraph.

Its potential departure would be the latest in a string of exits by companies seeking deeper pools of capital and higher valuations in the US.

In recent years, the equipment rental company Ashtead, the building material supplier CRH, and the owner of Paddy Power, Flutter Entertainment, have all moved their primary listings to the US.

The UK’s biggest drugmaker, AstraZeneca, listed its shares directly on the New York Stock Exchange this year, putting its US shares on an even footing with its London-listed stock.

A string of companies have also left London’s stock market after agreeing to takeover deals. The flurry of deal-making this year includes warehouse landlord Segro’s £14bn takeover by its US rival Prologis, easyJet’s £5.7bn takeover by the US private equity company Apollo and the £9.9bn takeover of asset manager Schroders by a US investor.

Other deals include the £10bn takeover of the lab testing group Intertek by a consortium led by the Swedish private equity company EQT in June. Beazley, the specialist insurer with clients including Lloyds of London, agreed an £8bn deal to be acquired by its larger rival Zurich in February.

Meanwhile, fewer companies are joining London’s stock market too, as the UK faces a dearth of flotations. There were just seven listings in the first half of this year, raising £577m in total, according to data from the professional services company EY.

Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, has been one of the few companies to join London’s market this year. The payments processor listed at £1.96 a share in October and traded at about £2.05 on Monday.

Compass was approached for comment.

items.body: Party that won just 0.2% of the vote in 2016 is on course for almost 20% this time and could be part of next government Almost exactly eight years ago, a video clip of a stocky, bearded man riding a horse through western Andalucía went viral in Spain . The rider was Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, the soundtrack was a bombastic snatch of the Lord of the Rings score, and the caption was an equally unsubtle callback to the 700-year fight to wrest the Iberian peninsula from Islamic rule. “La Reconquista comenzará en tierras andaluzas,” it read – the reconquest will begin on Andalucían soil. Celebrated by some, jeered by others – and inventively lampooned by those with sufficient skill and time on their hands – the video didn’t seem quite as amusing three weeks later when Vox broke through into the political mainstream by winning 12 seats in Andalucía’s regional parliament. Saying that the proliferation of quangos and other simi…

A badger sett in Hambledon, Surrey. Haigh did not push back against the idea Natural England was being targeted for abolition. Photograph: Lillian King/Getty Images

Natural England could be abolished as part of quango cull, says Louise Haigh

First secretary of state says proliferation of arms-length government bodies is hampering decision-making

The nature watchdog Natural England could be abolished as part of a cull of arm’s length government organisations, Louise Haigh has said.

Saying that the proliferation of quangos and other similar bodies had made decision-making by ministers more difficult, the first secretary of state said it could fall within a push to change the landscape of government by scrapping some organisations and bringing others into departments.

Abolishing Natural England could be justified on the basis that it could speed up planning decisions and thus boost housebuilding and growth, but removing or curbing its role would be likely to prompt concern from environmental groups.

Last month, the Conservatives announced that if they won power they would abolish both Natural England and the Environment Agency, saying this would help create more new homes.

Louise Haigh: ‘We’re absolutely committed to devolving responsibilities where they can be devolved.’ Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA

Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, was speaking before a speech to the CBI conference on Monday morning at which she was to make the case for greater government control of public utilities.

After the Times reported Natural England was in line to be abolished, Haigh was asked on Sky News about the proliferation of quangos. She said: “We’ve had successive governments complain about this, but unfortunately, successive governments have created more of these and pushed more decision-making out of their own departments, so that then when they make decisions they don’t agree with, they turn around and look in horror.

“That’s why we’re absolutely committed to devolving responsibilities where they can be devolved.”

Asked if she was considering getting rid of Natural England, she said: “We’re considering all arm’slength bodies, both devolving, dissolving, and bringing back into departments, because we cannot continue with this situation where politicians look round and can’t take responsibility for the actions that people have elected their government for.”

Asked again about the specific fate of Natural England in a later interview on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Haigh again did not push back against the idea it was being targeted for abolition along with other arms-length bodies.

She said: “So all the ALBs are in my sight for either devolving responsibilities that can be pushed down to mayors and strategic authorities, whether they can be brought back into departments under the direct power of the secretary of state, or whether they can be dissolved entirely.”

In a section of her speech about utilities, according to extracts released in advance, Haigh was to say she would “put pragmatism and public interest ahead of failed political ideology”, adding: “Public control is not anti-business – it’s about getting the foundations right, so that private enterprise can do what it does best.”

Saying almost no other nation had so many essential services run by private companies, and often overseas ones at that, Haigh was to say: “The status quo is not the neutral, pragmatic centre ground. It’s the outlier. An exception that no other nation is trying to emulate.”

Capita has adjusted operating profit forecasts for 2027, now out at £85m-£95m lower than previously thought, due to extra costs administering the UK Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) contract. Photograph: SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty Images

Capita boss exits and shares crash after civil service pensions failures

Price plunges 67% as Adolfo Hernandez leaves with ‘immediate effect’ amid continued fallout from pension payment problems

The boss of troubled outsourcing group Capita has abruptly departed as he admitted it has “not delivered” for retired civil servants left waiting for pension payments.

Chief executive Adolfo Hernandez has agreed with the firm’s board to step down with “immediate effect”, it said on Monday. He will be replaced by chief financial officer Pablo Andres for the top job.

Shares in Capita plunged by 67% to as low as 80p, Capita’s lowest share price since October 1991, on Monday morning as it cut profit forecasts and proposed raising £190m in extra capital.

Capita said that adjusted operating profit in 2027 is expected to be £85m to £95m lower than previously expected, due to extra costs in relation to the UK Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) contract, and “short-term contract headwinds”.

Pensioners have reported being forced to borrow money from family to pay for food and heating, with some saying they feared losing their homes because they could not afford their rent or mortgage.

The reshuffle comes after Capita got into hot water for delays in administering the 1.7 million member pension scheme, leaving thousands of civil servants waiting for payments and retirement quotes.

Capita, which has government contracts across education and defence, and collects the TV licence fee, agreed the pension contract with the former Conservative government in 2023. It came into force in December 2025.

The company has taken a hit to its finances as a result of the issues delivering the scheme and the implementation of a recovery plan.

It also faced a grilling by MPs in parliament last month, with one Cabinet Office minister labelling the company’s progress in improving how it runs the scheme as “abysmal”.

Hernandez said he recognised the shortcomings that had affected members of the pension scheme.

He said: “It has been a privilege to lead Capita through this phase of its transformation. Three years ago we set out to turn Capita into a technology led, AI-enabled business services company.

“I am proud of the groundwork we have laid and the progress we have made under my leadership.

“Of course, within that I recognise that we have not delivered the service that members of the civil service pension scheme deserve.”

The Guardian first reported on concerns over the pension scheme last year, and earlier this year the government admitted retired civil servants have been failed by the decision to outsource their pension scheme.

after newsletter promotion

Multiple members of the CSPS scheme then came forward to say they were unable to afford rent and have been forced to use food banks after being left without an income.

In July, the Cabinet Office confirmed it is hoping to take the scheme back in-house after “unacceptable” service levels.

Last week, Capita said: “We know that some members have been experiencing challenges with the [CSPS]. We’re very sorry for any delays and the frustration this is causing.”

MPs have blamed the problems on operational failures including overwhelmed revision teams, poor technology and incorrect pension quotes.

The company plans to raise the £190m in the first half of next year, “to reduce leverage and to allow the business to move forward from a more stable foundation”. The decision was supported by its biggest shareholder, the activist investor Oasis Management Company, it said.

Capita boss exits and shares crash after civil service pensions failures
Price plunges 67% as Adolfo Hernandez leaves with ‘immediate effect’ amid continued fallout from pension payment problems
The boss of troubled outsourcing group Capita has abruptly departed as he admitted it has “not delivered” for retired civil servants left waiting for pension payments.
Chief executive Adolfo Hernandez has agreed with the firm’s board to step down with “immediate effect”, it said on Monday. He will be replaced by chief financial officer Pablo Andres for the top job.
Shares in Capita plunged by 67% to as low as 80p, Capita’s lowest share price since October 1991, on Monday morning as it cut profit forecasts and proposed raising £190m in extra capital.

Capita said that adjusted operating profit in 2027 is expected to be £85m to £95m lower than previously expected, due to extra costs in relation to the UK Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) contract, and “short-term contract headwinds”.
Pensioners have reported being forced to borrow money from family to pay for food and heating, with some saying they feared losing their homes because they could not afford their rent or mortgage.
The reshuffle comes after Capita got into hot water for delays in administering the 1.7 million member pension scheme, leaving thousands of civil servants waiting for payments and retirement quotes.

Capita, which has government contracts across education and defence, and collects the TV licence fee, agreed the pension contract with the former Conservative government in 2023. It came into force in December 2025.
The company has taken a hit to its finances as a result of the issues delivering the scheme and the implementation of a recovery plan.
It also faced a grilling by MPs in parliament last month, with one Cabinet Office minister labelling the company’s progress in improving how it runs the scheme as “abysmal”.
Hernandez said he recognised the shortcomings that had affected members of the pension scheme.
He said: “It has been a privilege to lead Capita through this phase of its transformation. Three years ago we set out to turn Capita into a technology led, AI-enabled business services company.
“I am proud of the groundwork we have laid and the progress we have made under my leadership.
“Of course, within that I recognise that we have not delivered the service that members of the civil service pension scheme deserve.”

The Guardian first reported on concerns over the pension scheme last year, and earlier this year the government admitted retired civil servants have been failed by the decision to outsource their pension scheme.

Multiple members of the CSPS scheme then came forward to say they were unable to afford rent and have been forced to use food banks after being left without an income.
In July, the Cabinet Office confirmed it is hoping to take the scheme back in-house after “unacceptable” service levels.

items.body:
Lollipop people have to contend with limited hours, relatively low pay and the risk of encountering aggressive drivers. Photograph: Joshua Bright/The Guardian

Lollipop people have to contend with limited hours, relatively low pay and the risk of encountering aggressive drivers. Photograph: Joshua Bright/The Guardian

Fears for school crossing patrols as councils struggle to recruit lollipop people

Future of familiar school-run figures uncertain as vacancies surge and town halls consider alternatives

They have been a feature of British schooldays for decades, instantly recognisable by their round signs and yellow hi-vis uniforms. But a struggle to recruit against a backdrop of staff cuts at cash-strapped local authorities is threatening to make lollipop people a thing of the past.

The Recruitment and Employment Confederation (REC) said school crossing patrols were among jobs showing the biggest increase in vacancies in recent weeks, alongside sales roles and exam invigilators.

There is no legal obligation on councils to fill the roles. Last week, East Riding of Yorkshire council said a quarter of school crossing patrol sites were unstaffed, adding that applicant numbers were dwindling. It said it was exploring long-term alternatives at some sites, including infrastructure changes, such as creating zebra crossings.

Parents and carers in Hessle told the BBC that unstaffed crossings were “not really safe for the children”, but the council said some had been vacant for some time “with no applicants”, while others had become vacant after previous lollipop people retired.

A council spokesperson said: “The role of a school crossing patrol may not be as attractive in this day and age, as it requires work for limited hours each school day, offers relatively low pay for the short morning and afternoon shifts they are needed to work, and they are outside in all weathers.

“The short period of time they are needed to work may not suit everyone and limits what people can do during the rest of the day. But we continue to encourage local residents to apply for these jobs and help make a difference to children, parents and the school community.”

Earlier this year, after a council meeting in Redcar and Cleveland where elected representatives expressed concerns about gaps in school crossing patrols, the council leader, Alec Brown, said it was not easy to maintain a full roster.

“It’s difficult, you just can’t have a pool of ready-made lollipop people to step up,” he said after the meeting in March.

A Redcar and Cleveland borough council spokesperson said it advertised vacancies through the council’s recruitment channels and, where appropriate, directly through schools.

“We receive a reasonable number of applications, but one of the main challenges is that these roles are part-time positions with relatively low weekly hours,” the spokesperson added. “We currently have three applicants going through the recruitment process, and once appointed, the service will only have one vacancy remaining.”

The Bournemouth East MP, Tom Hayes, who has been campaigning to save local school crossing patrols, said: “I absolutely think we could be seeing the loss of lollipop people everywhere in the country. It just feels to me like we’re breaking down as a society so many of these touch points, which can hold communities together, the kind of the little things that create the glue.”

The factors of limited hours and low pay have probably been compounded in recent years by an increase in lollipop people facing dangerous and aggressive drivers, leading some councils to provide their crossing patrols with body cameras.

Ally Mitchell in his school crossing patrol uniform.

Ally Mitchell took a job as a lollipop person in Edinburgh after being made redundant from a role in the video games industry. It was initially meant to be a stopgap while he looked for a full-time position, but he enjoyed the job so much he stayed on even after securing a role in the charity sector.

“While the additional income is certainly important, what keeps me doing the job is the sense that I’ve become a trusted and respected member of my local community,” he said. “I genuinely enjoy helping people, wishing them a good morning and making a positive contribution to their day.”

Mitchell said school crossing patrols go “beyond road safety”, having a wider impact on communities. “I think we’re living in a world where people can increasingly feel isolated and disconnected from one another,” he said.

“School crossing patrol officers are one of those little everyday points of human contact that help bring communities together.

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

“You can replace a crossing with road markings or traffic lights, but you can’t necessarily replace the person standing there, remembering the children’s names, greeting their families and becoming part of their lives,” he added. “And I think that would be a real loss.”

Meanwhile, in some areas, those who want to become a lollipop person may struggle to find work, with councils scrapping the positions to save money.

Last year, Durham council – controlled by Reform UK – decided to scrap vacant roles for crossing guards as part of a savings drive, saying: “These posts have been vacant for a prolonged period of time without incident.”

The latest data available, obtained by the GMB trade union under freedom of information laws, found that school crossing patrol officer numbers in England, Scotland and Wales fell by 2,081 in a decade, from 7,128 in 2009-10 to 5,047 in 2017-18.

Earlier this year, Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole council postponed its proposed cuts to patrols after a campaign was launched to save the roles.

The council took the decision to “upgrade” school crossing patrol sites with permanent crossings in 2024.

A council spokesperson said: “While we appreciate there is the loss of a familiar face in the community, permanent crossings provide a safe and reliable facility that is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, benefiting schoolchildren and the wider community all year round.”

Hayes said the issue was part of a broader pattern. “Whether it’s the librarian behind the counter, who’s going to help you to do your homework, whether it’s the person who works at a Sure Start centre who’s going to help you to raise your kid because they give you the skills that you need, whether it’s the playground that’s broken down, where mums would otherwise have just sat on a bench for ages and got to know each other, there are these just little contact points in the society.

“If you chip away at them, and you do it in the interest of saving money, or you’re doing it in the interest of something more efficient, which are the arguments I have heard, it just undermines who we are as a society, and it makes it harder for people to feel like they can create connection.”

items.title: Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore ties after tensions over conflict
items.summary: The two leaders committed to upholding sovereignty and "non-interference in the internal affairs of states".
items.body:
Image source, William Ruto/X

Image caption,

The meeting between Kenya's President William Ruto (left) and DR Congo's Félix Tshisekedi (centre) was hosted by Denis Sassou Nguesso (right)

ByBasillioh Rukanga

Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.

This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.

On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".

The agreement was announced in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé as mediator.

Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".

DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).

DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.

DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.

When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was launched in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.

The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.

DR Congo said naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.

• Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader Published31 October

Relations deteriorated further after Kenya hosted a meeting of Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila, in October 2025.

Kabila was in 2025 sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself.

He has since been named the leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), the new rebel coalition that took over from the AFC.

Sunday's meeting between Ruto and Tshisekedi also included other issues including deepening trade cooperation, economic development, and regional integration.

The two also sought to collaborate to control the spread of the Ebola virus.

On Sunday, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said the frequency of attacks across the country's east had increased since the end of October, seriously affecting the Ebola response.

Tedros said heavy fighting in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged had disrupted work and the wider Ebola response.

More than 5,700 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.

The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.

items.title: Gas prices in Europe surge as forecast cold snap feeds supply shortage fears
items.summary: Jump in price follows slowdown in Qatar supplies and depleted summer stocks due to heatwaves Business live – latest updates European gas prices surged on Monday as a forecast cold snap in the coming weeks fed fears across the continent’s over depleted supply this winter and costly household bills. T…
items.body:
A cold snap is forecast across north-west Europe. Photograph: John Potter/Alamy

A cold snap is forecast across north-west Europe. Photograph: John Potter/Alamy

Gas prices in Europe surge as forecast cold snap feeds supply shortage fears

Jump in price follows slowdown in Qatar supplies and depleted summer stocks due to heatwaves

• Business live – latest updates

European gas prices surged on Monday as a forecast cold snap in the coming weeks fed fears across the continent’s over depleted supply this winter and costly household bills.

The Dutch month-ahead contract – the European benchmark for gas prices over the next four weeks– rose by as much as 8.6% to €96.08, before settling up 4% at €92.50.

The jump in gas prices comes as much of north-west Europe braces for a tough winter, when energy demand is at its highest.

Europe’s gas supplies have been hit by a slowdown in exports from Qatar due to the war in the Middle East, as well as an increase in consumption during the summer to power refrigeration and cooling during the prolonged heatwave.

Storage levels on the continent are now well below the seasonal average, at about 69% full against a typical level of 80%.

Labour faces double blow over UK fossil fuel projects

Read more

In the UK, energy system operators have said the country will have enough gas and electricity to meet demand during the coldest months, partly because of paying higher market prices than neighbours to secure imports.

However, it means British households will probably pay some of the highest energy bills in Europe this winter.

This week the energy regulator Ofgem is expected to announce a 26% rise in its quarterly price cap from January, adding an extra £443 to an average annual bill for a dual-fuel household.

It could be one of the biggest quarterly price rises on record. The charity Citizens Advice has said it expects a wave of more people seeking emergency help.

The chief executive, Clare Moriarty, said every day its “advisers see people whose budgets have been completely wiped out by years of compounding crises.”

“Millions of households are entering the coldest months of the year with nothing left,” she said.

Last month, the chancellor, John Healey, used his first budget to announce a giveaway of £100 to 20m households in council tax bands A to D to help with energy bills.

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

But Moriarty said that, while the top-up was welcome, it “simply won’t stretch far enough for those who need the most support.”

“Many households will quickly burn through it, leaving them at risk of deeper debt or being unable to top up their prepayment meter just as winter bites.

“The government must take action before the cold weather takes hold. A targeted top-up to the warm home discount and an emergency support credit for prepayment customers are vital, practical lifelines that will stop households being left in the cold and dark this winter.”

Chris O’Shea, the boss of British Gas owner Centrica, has also said he is “hugely concerned” about the forecast jump in energy bills, warning that the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their bills would rise in the new year.

He told the BBC on Sunday that there is a “massive problem” with people not paying their bills in the UK, with some without the means to do so and an “increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills”.

items.title: Burnham to tell MPs 'landmark' EU deal could make next decade 'much better'
items.summary: The prime minister will tell MPs the deal agreed on Friday is a "choice between a broken status quo or change".
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Andy Burnham agreed a deal with the EU in Brussels on Friday

ByNick Eardley, Political correspondent and Matt Spivey

The prime minister will tell Parliament on Monday the "landmark" deal struck with the EU means there is a "very real prospect" the next decade can be "much better" than the last one.

The deal is a "choice between a broken status quo or change", Andy Burnham will tell MPs.

He will also call it "the single biggest growth measure to be delivered in this parliament" - repeating his claim it could add £17bn to the British economy.

The PM described it on Friday as a "win-win" deal with the EU on British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. But since then a host of politicians have criticised the plan, with one former prime minister urging him to "move on" from Brexit.

Burnham believes the agreement reached in Brussels "holds out the very real prospect that the next decade can be a much better one for Britain than the one we have just lived through".

"The ability to draw a line on a decade of drift and division is in our hands and I believe we should take it," he will say in his speech.

He will also paint the move as a choice "between easing pressure on the cost of living or allowing food prices to rise further" and "creating opportunities for young people or denying them".

He believes polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

But his announcement on Friday was greeted with a chorus of criticism from a number of opposing political figures.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was unfair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels.

She questioned the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".

Badenoch accused him of having "plucked that figure out of the air" before saying "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".

Meanwhile Reform UK leader Farage called the deal a "very good day for the EU", before adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."

Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added in a social media post: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."

Over the weekend former prime ministers including Theresa May, Sir Tony Blair and Rishi Sunak also criticised the EU-UK deal.

May, who presided over three years of Brexit negotiations during her premiership, said she was "aghast" by the deal and warned Andy Burnham should "move on".

Sir Tony, who was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, told The Sunday Times Britain should only rejoin the EU if it reforms, and allows more innovation on technology.

Badenoch will use her speech at the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) annual conference on Monday to criticise Burnham's EU deal.

She will accuse the prime minister of securing a "terrible" deal and will say he should be "aiming a lot higher" in terms of driving growth.

Farage will tell the same conference that establishing closer ties with the EU would be a "disaster" for British businesses.

Rejoining the EU will hit the small firms that do not even trade with Europe with more red tape, more compliance costs, more Brussels rules they never asked for, he is expected to say.

On Friday, the PM said that over the coming months both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at the options for the UK's "long-term relationship" with the EU.

He was also clear that the deal he struck was "probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it".

He added: "But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."

items.body:
Image source, Planet Labs PBC

Image caption,

Satellite imagery showed a ship on fire early on Sunday morning

ByHafsa Khalil

Updated 4 minutes ago

An explosion has occurred on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port after a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.

The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.

It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.

Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.

Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.

The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.

Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.

GNS said the country was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.

Seperately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.

GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".

Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.

items.title: Trump hosts third crypto gala for meme coin amid conflict of interest outcry
items.summary: Virginia dinner comes as Democrats accuse president of improperly profiting from his cryptocurrency ventures Donald Trump has headlined his third cryptocurrency gala at his ​country club in Virginia, rewarding top holders of his own meme coin, as Democrats accuse the president of improperly profitin…
items.body:
Donald Trump gestures to reporters while taking questions during a news briefing in the White House on Friday in Washington DC. Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Donald Trump gestures to reporters while taking questions during a news briefing in the White House on Friday in Washington DC. Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Trump hosts third crypto gala for meme coin amid conflict of interest outcry

Virginia dinner comes as Democrats accuse president of improperly profiting from his cryptocurrency ventures

Donald Trump is scheduled to headline his third cryptocurrency gala on ⁠Sunday night at his ​country club in Virginia, rewarding top holders of his own meme coin as Democrats accuse the president of improperly profiting from his crypto ventures.

The dinner, set to take place at the Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, will include meet-and-greets with Trump supporters including the boxing champion Floyd Mayweather, Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary, NBA champion Tristan Thompson and mentalist Lior Suchard, according to the event’s website.

The gala’s access and perks are divided by tiers for the 185 holders of $TRUMP, the president’s meme coin. A Trump fragrance, a poster, a “commemorative” ticket, and a “Trump watch” are reserved for 120 attendees. Meanwhile, the top 29 investors are invited to a VIP reception, and the top four will receive a “TRUMP 18K Gold Watch”.

Trump has hosted two similar galas since he took office last year, bringing a flurry of criticism as Democrats accuse Trump and his family of monetizing his brand through an array of equities and crypto ventures while in office.

A statue of Donald Trump holding a bitcoin in recognition of his support for cryptocurrency is displayed on the National Mall in September 2025 in Washington DC. Photograph: Alex Brandon/AP

After sweepingwins in the midterms, Democrats have vowed to investigate conflicts of interest involving Trump and his personal wealth during his presidency. They also say they plan to push for legislation that would ban activities such as the meme coin gala dinner.

“This dinner and scoring mechanism appear carefully constructed to increase investment in $TRUMP, allowing the President to abuse the power of his office to personally enrich himself, as he has throughout this term,” reads a letter sent by Adam Schiff and eight other US senators last month.

Since returning to the White House, Trump has made more than $1bn from his crypto businesses, according to financial disclosures released in June. Trump received more than $500m from his World Liberty Financial business selling new crypto products, and raked another $600m from sales of souvenir-type “meme” coins stamped with Trump’s face. Trump launched his $Trump meme coin days before his inauguration.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Interest in the $TRUMP coin dinner has plummeted, with contestants’ combined holdings dropping from $148m in May 2025 to $8.6m in this month’s gala.

More than half of the digital wallets publicly listed on the contest leaderboard for Sunday’s dinner are tied directly to crypto exchanges that bar US-based users, indicating they ‌are linked to foreign nationals, according to an analysis of blockchain data prepared for Reuters by the nonpartisan, non-profit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.

Demonstrators hold up mock cryptocurrency during a rally Against Trump's crypto dealings at the Trump National Golf Club in May 2025 in Virginia. Photograph: Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Public Citizen

“Neither the President nor his family ⁠has ever engaged — or will ever engage — in conflicts of interest,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Reuters ​earlier this year. “President Trump proudly made ​the United States the crypto capital of the world ​through executive actions.“

The Trump family’s other crypto-connected equities and ventures have also fallen in value to record ​lows. Together, outside investors in their ‌five main crypto and ​crypto-linked projects have lost more than $5bn​, according to a Reuters analysis.

The Trump meme coin has earned the Trump family at least $635m, according to the president’s June financial disclosure statement. In total, the Trumps had earned at least $2.3bn through April from their four main crypto ventures, including the meme coin.

The president’s stake in a fifth crypto-linked venture, Trump Media & Technology Group, is worth about $430m.

Reuters contributed reporting

items.summary: Jetstar accused of issuing customers credits instead of cash refunds for flights cancelled between 2020 and late 2022 Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast More than 1 million Jetstar customers could be eligible to join a class action alleging the airline failed to refund them…
items.body:
Echo Law is leading a class action against Jetstar over allegations it failed to refund customers for cancelled flights during the pandemic. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

Echo Law is leading a class action against Jetstar over allegations it failed to refund customers for cancelled flights during the pandemic. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

Up to 1.1m people eligible to join class action against Jetstar over alleged failure to refund Covid flights

Jetstar accused of issuing customers credits instead of cash refunds for flights cancelled between 2020 and late 2022

• Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

More than 1 million Jetstar customers could be eligible to join a class action alleging the airline failed to refund them for flights it cancelled during the pandemic, the firm leading the lawsuit has said.

The federal court on Monday confirmed it had ordered notices be sent to customers informing them of their eligibility to participate in, or opt out of, the lawsuit, with a potential trial set for March 2027.

Echo Law, the firm leading the class action, said it wanted to alert the public to the notices – which were due to be distributed by 4 December – to ensure they understood it was not a scam. About 1.1 million people will receive them.

The class action alleges Jetstar issued customers flight credits instead of the cash refunds they were entitled to for flights cancelled between 2020 and late 2022, after cancelling thousands of scheduled domestic and international flights.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email

Echo Law ran a separate class action against Qantas over its handling of Covid-19 travel credits, which the airline in March agreed to settle for $105m with no admission of liability.

In its case against Jetstar, the firm alleges the airline breached its legal obligations to customers by failing to provide refunds for cancelled flights, instead offering customers credit vouchers.

It alleges Jetstar misled customers and engaged in unconscionable conduct in breach of Australian consumer law.

It also alleges that, by holding customers’ funds that ought to have been refunded, Jetstar unlawfully benefited from this conduct.

Jetstar has denied the allegations and is defending the class action

“During the Covid-19 pandemic, Jetstar took a range of steps to respond to rapidly changing travel restrictions, while continuing to support customers affected by disruptions,” a spokesperson for the airline said.

“We provided customers with a range of options during this period depending on the circumstances, including travel credits, fee-free flight changes and refunds.

They said customers with a Jetstar Covid-19 voucher could use it whenever they were ready to, as the airline had removed the expiry date in 2023.

However, Andrew Paull, a partner at Echo Law, alleged Jetstar’s policy of “pushing” customers to accept vouchers was designed to preserve the airline’s cash position.

“It held onto ordinary Australian’s [sic] money and expected customers to just be happy with credits, or in some cases nothing, when we allege they were entitled to cash refunds,” he alleged.

Paull alleged many customers had ended up paying Jetstar more than their original booking to use their credits on new fares, as they were led to believe they had little choice but to do so in order to avoid losing the value of their flights.

The firm’s lawsuit against Jetstar is scheduled for mediation in December and is expected to go to trial if the parties fail to reach an agreement.

Echo Law said the litigation funder Court House Capital was backing its class action against Jetstar.

Court House Capital’s chief investment officer, Heather Collins, accused Jetstar of seeking to “delay resolution while continuing to hold onto money that belongs to Australian families”.

items.summary: Gate fee comes on top of annual cost of between $300 and $700 per family Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Football clubs representing hundreds of thousands of players are preparing to break away from Football Queensland this week, saying the state governing body charges u…
items.body:
Many Queensland football club members say the state governing body, Football Queensland, charges unreasonably high fees and is unaccountable. Photograph: Natee127/Getty Images

Many Queensland football club members say the state governing body, Football Queensland, charges unreasonably high fees and is unaccountable. Photograph: Natee127/Getty Images

Clubs and families revolt as Football Queensland charges $5 a head to watch children play

Gate fee comes on top of annual cost of between $300 and $700 per family

• Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Football clubs representing hundreds of thousands of players are preparing to break away from Football Queensland this week, saying the state governing body charges unreasonably high fees and is unaccountable.

Some parents and siblings are charged a $5 gate fee to watch children’s matches in parts of regional Queensland.

The gate fee comes on top of an annual cost of between $300 and $700 per family, depending on player age, club and other factors, and a range of other fees, fines and charges. Many football club members say they see little in return for the thousands they pay in fees.

Jessy Mulla is president of Leichhardt Football Club Cairns Incorporated, which was recently disaffiliated from the statewide body.

Football Queensland, which manages the club, introduced a gate fee in 2024 in order to pay for improvements to the ground, Endeavour Park, in Manunda, such as cleaning toilets, employing a full-time gardener, and “increased shade structures and grandstands”, at a quoted price of $20,000 each.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email

With a few hundred people attending most weekends, the amount raised through gate fees must be substantial, Mulla said.

But there had been “very, very” little improvement to the ground since, Mulla said.

“That’s why everyone asks where’s the money being spent? Where’s the money that gets raised? Where is it going?”

Under Football Queensland’s policy, registered coaches and team managers, referees, volunteers and children under 15 enter free. Pensioners get a discount, paying $4.

The sport’s governing body in the state is a member of the national football body, Football Australia. It provides a range of services for typically volunteer-run clubs, including managing competitions, governance, and developing player professional pathways, as well as managing some facilities.

Clubs have to pay an annual fee to affiliate with the central body, which they pass on to players.

A spokesperson for Football Queensland said the body was “continuing to progress the delivery and investment of long-term infrastructure projects and facility enhancements” in line with its regional facility master plan.

The spokesperson said three levels of government had invested $7.9m into regional Football Queensland facilities since 2023. The central body had also contributed $4.9m in operational costs and capital investment in regional Queensland during the same period, they said.

“A $5 gate fee (or $80 season pass) is consistent with other sporting codes and contributes to FQ’s master plan delivery, helping to offset grounds maintenance and operational expenses,” they said.

It recently created controversy by proposing to charge a $35 per player fee for summer competitions organised by the clubs themselves, and proposing other fee increases, which have since been dropped.

A rebel faction of football clubs is preparing to break away from Football Queensland this week, complaining of a lack of input and transparency of the central body.

items.body: In today’s newsletter: The prime minister has reopened the debate over a future relationship with a changed EU – as the bloc faces the rise of the far right, a protectionist economic agenda and growing defence ambitions Good morning. Nobody really wants to think about Brexit any more, save for the original Brexiters, who seem delighted that Andy Burnham’s “reset” with the EU has given them an excuse to get the old gang back together. But arguments about whether the UK should rejoin the EU will reignite in parliament this week, as Burnham briefs MPs on the deal he agreed on Friday. That deal wasn’t so much a victory as the culmination of Keir Starmer’s incrementalist approach to UK-EU relations. Its core agreements haven’t been ratified by member states yet, and the EU won’t sign them off until Britain resolves a dispute over tuition fees for European students. Burnham is apparently “determined” to take the UK back into the EU, but don’t expect any progress on that before the next general election. Cop 31 | The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal that “failed to meet the moment” in a dramatic finish to the UN talks in Turkey. The proposed deal failed to endorse a away from fossil fuels that more than 130 countries demanded. Russia | A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack , causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel. Weapons | The Red Cross and other rights groups have warned that it will soon be too late to properly regulate the development of autonomous weapons. The warning came as the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons concluded without an agreement on an instrument for regulating autonomous weapons. UK news | Dozens of hospitals are so short of money they may not be able to continue caring for patients and are being forced to make “unpalatable” cuts to services and staff, the Guardian can reveal.

items.title: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
items.summary: The COP31 summit in Antalya was the longest-running climate talks in UN history.
items.body:
Image source, Chris McGrath/Getty Images

ByJustin Rowlatt, Climate editor and Esme Stallard, Senior climate and science journalist, Reporting fromAntalya, Turkey

The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 bought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.

The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.

Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.

After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.

Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".

The world is preparing for life beyond 1.5C

This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.

The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.

Without agreement, that recognition has been lost.

Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:

• Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding, external

• The ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine life

• Extreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the world

Image source, Anil Shakya/AFP/Getty Images

Image caption,

In a 2C world extreme heat is expected to be experienced in every inhabitated area on Earth

Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.

"This COP sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.

The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible – it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).

This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.

Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.

There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial, external and are not well advanced.

Countries divided over approach on fossil fuels

This year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.

On the central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts – countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.

And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.

Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.

This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.

If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.

• Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposedPublished3 hours ago

Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago.

"The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory".

That was made apparent during the final meeting when pointed remarks were delivered. EU representative Darragh O'Brien said the talks had been "hijacked by some oil states".

Russian delegate Sergei Kononuchenko switched from Russian to English to directly address the EU delegation. He accused them of providing climate finance only in the form of loans to developing nations: "This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner".

It is a serious blow not just to climate action, but to multilateralism itself - the idea that countries can put aside their differences on other issues to tackle problems they can't solve alone.

COP31 had some good news

Much of the coverage of COP31 has focused on the failure to get the central political agreement passed.

But much of the work at these summits is putting into action agreements made at previous meetings.

On money that is going towards adaptation for example, countries need to agree how is it being distributed, is it making an impact and how can this be tracked, and which areas are particularly vulnerable.

In fact, there were 164 other items on this year's agenda that were being thrashed out in the negotiating rooms.

And some of those were agreed at the talks.

The funds raised from a global system of carbon credits – money given in exchange for releasing greenhouse gases – will go towards helping developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change.

They agreed to advance a just transition framework designed to protect workers and communities as global economies shift toward clean energy.

But there were many more that could not be agreed and some will now be picked up at COP32, including crucially the work programme responsible for driving forward action on cutting emissions.

Renewable energy growth remains unstoppable

What governments agree in the COP negotiating rooms is only part of what determines the speed of the energy transition.

The International Energy Agency's latest World Energy Outlook, external points to another powerful force: energy security.

It says the disruption to oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz has been the biggest energy supply shock in history. The longer the uncertainty continues, the stronger the incentive for countries to switch from imported fossil fuels to electricity generated at home.

Image source, Costfoto/NurPhoto/Getty Images

Image caption,

Renewable energy capacity is expected to grow 60% more over the next six-year period than the previous

The economics have been changing too.

Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles have become increasingly competitive.

As clean energy develops its own commercial momentum, formal negotiations may become less important in determining its direction and pace.

Against the headwinds of inflation new investment announcements emerged at COP as part of the "Action Agenda".

This is the part of the COP process that tries to mobilise action outside of formal talks from businesses, investors and cities – this year the focus was on electrification. Turning more of our energy from fossil fuels to electricity.

"We are not entering the age of electricity, we have arrived at the age of electricity," Fatih Birol, head of the IEA, told the BBC. He says energy security and climate policies are now "closely aligned".

That doesn't make COP irrelevant.

Governments still have a crucial role in facilitating the transition, according to Dr Jennie Dodson, a senior director at the World Business Council for Sustainable Development which includes among its members the likes of Amazon and Apple.

"A key message from business is we can go so far, a lot of it is cost competitive, but there are policy barriers both around infrastructure and permitting".

Image source, Chris McGrath/Getty Images

Image caption,

Many are questioning whether the COP process is fit for purpose

The COP process needs to change

COP31 has shown how the role of these annual UN climate conferences is changing.

For the first 30 COPs, the emphasis was on building the international framework for tackling global warming.

The great diplomatic breakthrough came in Paris in 2015, when almost every country agreed to keep global warming well below 2°C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.

Paris also established machinery designed to turn promises into progress. Every five years, governments assess collective progress in a global stocktake and submit new national climate plans, known as NDCs.

Then came further agreements: a fund for climate damage at COP27, a commitment to transition away from fossil fuels and triple renewable energy capacity at COP28, a new climate finance target at COP29 and increased support for adaptation at COP30.

The international architecture for tackling climate change has, in other words, largely been built.

Now comes the harder business of making it work. That's why this year's conference in Antalya, Turkey, had been billed as an "implementation COP".

The emphasis now is shifting towards delivering commitments already made. Camilla Born, who helped develop the UK's strategy for COP26 and now heads the campaign group Electrify Britain, told the BBC this is making COP more procedural - less about fundamental negotiations than ensuring the machinery actually works.

This could mean doing away with a cover text – the central political agreement that countries sign up to with new pledges.

It is not a requirement to have one, and for many years countries managed without. Australia chose to push one for this COP, and it is where they fell down.

On many of the procedural issues Camilla Bonn spoke of, they did agree things. That may be important. It isn't necessarily exciting.

And there is a fundamental limit to what this machinery can achieve. Under the Paris Agreement countries have no mechanism to force them to meet their emissions targets.

So, when critics berate the COP process for failing to tackle the problem fast enough, it isn't really the system that is at fault, says Alden Meyer, a veteran climate negotiator now at the climate think tank E3G.

The COP process, he suggests, is "like a mirror that we hold up to ourselves every year". If the reflection is disappointing, the problem is the governments, not the mirror.

items.body:
The Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, about 50km from Jakarta, caught fire on Saturday afternoon. Photograph: Mohammad Hashemi Rafsanjani/AFP/Getty Images

The Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, about 50km from Jakarta, caught fire on Saturday afternoon. Photograph: Mohammad Hashemi Rafsanjani/AFP/Getty Images

Fire at confectionery factory in Indonesia leaves at least three dead and dozens missing

Relatives of the missing victims flocked to the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones

A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has killed three people with 36 remaining missing, an Indonesian rescue official says.

Drone footage showed large parts of the factory destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising from the complex. Photos and videos shared by rescuers show officers entering the charred building in search of the missing victims on Sunday, with small fires still burning in some spots.

Relatives of the missing victims flocked near the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones, footage aired by local broadcasters showed.

A drone view of emergency crews gathered outside the factory in Indonesia’s Banten province. Photograph: Reuters

The Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, located in Cikande in Indonesia’s Banten province about 50km from the capital, caught fire on Saturday afternoon, search and rescue official Rizky Dwianto said on Sunday.

“All elements of the joint SAR [search-and-rescue] team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritising the safety of personnel in the field,” he added.

Rizky said four people were injured and taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic.

Firefighters were alerted about 4.30pm on Saturday and found the building already engulfed in flames when they arrived, fire official Tubagus Machfudz told local broadcaster Kompas TV.

Smoke rises from the factory on Sunday. Photograph: Reuters

“When we arrived … a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company’s protection system was functioning properly or not,” he said.

The Banten province governor Andra Soni told reporters overnight that an estimated 60 people were inside the factory when it caught fire.

The cause of the incident is still under investigation, the local disaster agency said in an Instagram post on Sunday.

Crews from Indonesia’s Basarnas search and rescue agency inspect the site. Photograph: BASARNAS/AP

Deadly fires are not uncommon in Indonesia.

In December last year, a blaze that was likely caused by a drone battery explosion tore through a seven-storey building in Jakarta and killed at least 22 people, police said.

In 2023, at least 13 people were killed in the country’s east after an explosion at a nickel-processing plant.

A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has killed three people with 36 remaining missing, an Indonesian rescue official says.

What's next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?

What's next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?

The COP31 climate summit in Turkey has officially come to an end after countries failed to come to a consensus on a new deal.

The European Union and some other countries rejected a fourth draft agreement over its failure to mention a need to phase out fossil fuels, the largest driver of global climate change.

An EU representative accuses some oil states of hijacking talks, as Russia defends opposing the inclusion of such a commitment and levels direct criticism at the EU in its speech.

The talks have been the longest-running in the summit's history, with negotiations breaking down two days after they had been due to end.

BBC climate and science reporter Esme Stallard reports from Antalya, in Turkey.

items.title: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say
items.summary: Eleven people are dead in the attack on Dymer, with rescue efforts ongoing to find those still missing from the residential building.
items.body:
Figure caption,

'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes hit Kyiv

ByHafsa Khalil

Updated 33 minutes ago

ByJessica Lamb

A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer after 14 hours, in overnight Russian strikes on Dymer, in the Kyiv region, that killed nine people, Ukrainian officials have said.

The attack occurred in the early hours of Sunday. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive from the collapsed building, Kyiv's regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.

A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike on Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, that hit a grocery store on Sunday.

Ukrainian authorities said the boy in Dymer is in stable condition and was taken to hospital, and have thanked everyone involved in saving his life.

Zelensky and Ukraine's national police also confirmed the rescue of the boy.

Response teams including police, explosive technicians, dog handlers and medics are continuing with rescue efforts.

In a telegram post, Tkachenko said the 79-year-old woman rescued from the rubble was receiving treatment in hospital.

Earlier he said six people were injured in the attack, while others were still missing.

Image source, Ukraine State Emergency Service

Image caption,

The attack on the residential building occurred in the early hours of the morning while people were asleep

Zelensky said more than 130 people are involved in emergency operations at the scene, and that they will continue until they have "complete information about every single person".

Sending his condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed, he said the strike struck the residential building, "practically blowing a section of it to smithereens".

Zelensky added that "rescue efforts are complicated by constant new air raid alerts and renewed threats".

The strike hit the building at 05:00 local time, when families were still asleep, Ukraine's minister of internal affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi said.

More than 70 strikes have been launched across 10 Ukrainian regions as of Sunday evening, Vyhivskyi added.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Emergency workers continue to search for those missing after Russian drone and missile attacks in Dymer.

In his video address posted online, Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 injured in a strike on an "ordinary grocery store" in Vyshneve.

Tkachenko previously said two other people were killed and eight wounded in the Vyshneve attack.

Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukraine's Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said in a post on X., external

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
